$comment: ONE corpus, read by BOTH adapters. This file is the subject of the
conformance claim: 'the Python middleware and the Kong plugin enforce the
same contract' is only checkable if there is a single artefact they are
both checked against.
Two separate test suites, each written against its own implementation,
cannot establish this. They can both be green while disagreeing, because
each asserts what its own code does. That is the failure this file exists
to make impossible: a divergence fails a test rather than passing two.
Cases are grouped by the pure decision each adapter makes. Only pure
logic lives here — path matching, header classification, response
reading. Anything needing a network or a database belongs in the
integration suites, not in a corpus that must run identically in Lua and
Python.
corpus_version moves when a case stops being readable by a runner that
does not know about a new field, and the Lua runner asserts it. v3 added
require_signed_decisions to decide_response_signature: a v2 runner would
read the mandatory-mode case as if the mode were off and report it green
having asserted the opposite contract, which is precisely the silent
agreement this file exists to prevent.
A protected path guards a prefix boundary, not a string prefix. '/mcp'
must cover '/mcp' and everything below it, and must NOT cover a
different resource whose name merely starts with the same characters.
'/mcpfoo' and '/mcp-evil' are the cases that matter: a naive
startswith() accepts both, and an attacker who can name a route picks
exactly that shape. Getting it wrong sends unprotected traffic through
an enforcement point that believes it is enforcing.

cases.why: exact match
trailing slash is the same resource
descendant, separated by /
deep descendant
different resource; a prefix compare would accept it
different resource; hyphen is not a separator
different resource, even with a descendant
the root is not the protected surface
unrelated
the boundary is anchored at the start, not searched for

$comment: Reserved headers carry MudraID's own context to the upstream. A CALLER
supplying one is attempting to inject authority it was never granted,
so they are stripped before evaluation — every one of them, regardless
of case, because HTTP header names are case-insensitive and an
adapter that only stripped the lowercase spelling would strip nothing
an attacker actually sends.
How a /decide response becomes an enforcement outcome. 'error' means
the adapter could not read a trustworthy answer and must deny-close —
it is NEVER a quieter kind of allow.
expected_decision_id is the id the adapter sent. decided_at is
expressed as an offset in seconds from 'now' so the corpus does not
age: a literal timestamp would pass today and fail in a month.

cases.name: a bound allow is an allow
a bound deny is a deny
a bare allow is not an answer
cases.$why: five characters anything on the path could have produced

cases.name: an unsupported response contract is refused
an absent response contract is refused
an allow bound to another request is refused
cases.$why: the replay case: a genuine allow, answering someone else's question

cases.name: an absent decision id is refused
an unrecognised decision word is never optimistically read
capitalisation is not the vocabulary
a stale decision is refused
cases.$why: the id is echoed from the request, so replaying a whole exchange pairs a stale allow with a fresh-looking id

cases.name: a decision dated in the future is refused
a decision with no timestamp is refused
cases.$why: unbounded age; a captured allow would stay usable forever

cases.name: a small clock difference is tolerated
cases.$why: real clocks disagree; a decision is not the place to discover it

$comment: AUDIT-009 A9-02 — the /decide RESPONSE signature. Vectors are
minted by the REAL authority signer
(services/enforcement-service/app/application/decision_signature.py)
over an ephemeral RSA key whose PUBLIC half alone is stored below;
regenerate with scripts/generate_decision_signature_conformance.py.
Both runners inject verification_now as the verification clock, so
the pre-signed timestamps are deterministic and never age out.
outcome drives the Python runner (_read_decision, full pipeline).
signature_valid routes the LUA runner, it does not merely filter
it. true/false cases carry a signature and go to
decide.verify_signature, the pure verifier, which needs real
RS256 and therefore runs in the gateway image build. null cases
carry NO signature, so there is nothing for that verifier to
check; they go to decide.read_response instead, which is where
ABSENCE is governed, and which needs no RS256 and so runs
everywhere.
require_signed_decisions is the operator setting, spelled the way
BOTH adapters spell it. Absent means false. It is what makes the
two null cases a pair: one envelope, two modes, opposite
outcomes. lua_refusal_reason is asserted only by the Lua runner,
because the Kong adapter gives absence its own reason code while
the middleware returns an untyped error on both signature paths.

cases.name: an envelope flipped to allow under an intact deny signature is refused
cases.why: THE forgery this signature exists for: the unsigned envelope copy of every signed field must agree with the claims byte-for-byte

cases.name: an envelope with a rewritten reason under an intact signature is refused
cases.why: the stable reason code is a bound field; rewriting the envelope copy alone is a checkable mismatch

cases.name: another decision's genuine signature replayed onto this envelope is refused
cases.why: replay across decisions: the signed claims name dec-other, the envelope names dec-expected

cases.name: a signature naming an unpublished (retired) key is refused
cases.why: rotation refusal: a key that is no longer published is a key whose signatures are no longer trusted

cases.name: a signature produced with a different private key is refused
cases.why: the claims name the published key id but the bytes were signed by someone else's key

cases.name: claims naming a different key than the signature is refused
cases.why: a verifier resolves the key from the signature; claims that name another are unverifiable by construction

cases.name: algorithm 'none' is refused on the pinned constant
cases.why: the algorithm is compared against the pinned RS256, never read out of the signature and used

cases.name: an unsupported signature profile is refused
cases.why: a profile this verifier does not implement is one whose fields it cannot read; reading them anyway is how an allow gets believed

cases.name: a signature that is not valid base64 is refused
cases.why: malformed signature material is a refusal, never skipped

cases.name: a signature past its expires_at is refused
cases.why: a captured signed allow must stop working; the window is the backstop behind the decided_at freshness bound

cases.name: a signature not yet valid is refused
cases.why: a not_before in the future means a clock somewhere is wrong by more than the tolerated skew; refusing beats guessing

cases.name: a genuine signature bound to another platform is refused
cases.why: the signature verifies — MudraID really signed it — but it describes someone else's surface/request, which is a system failing at its own job if accepted

cases.name: an unsigned response is still read (verify-when-present)
cases.why: the authority activates signing by rollout; refusing every unsigned response would make activation a flag-day. This is the DEFAULT posture in both adapters, and it is 1.1-compatible: turning the requirement on is an operator's decision, not an upgrade's

cases.name: an unsigned response is refused when signing is required
cases.why: once the authority signs every response for a surface, an UNSIGNED one there is a STRIPPED signature — the exact thing the signature exists to detect — so reading it would leave a TLS-terminating party able to remove the protection by deleting a field. Refused with its own reason, not the invalid-signature one: 'no signature at all' is a stalled rollout and 'a signature that did not check out' is a key problem or an attack, and they lead an operator to opposite actions
